title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
text:
This page runs through some R-code examples of ways to examine the pre-baked ONS GVA and jobs data from here, which has been processed/linked to help smooth the path to getting GVA and jobs insights.
As well as base R and ggplot, it also uses a few bespoke functions written to analyse/visualise this data; these are all available in the project repo, in the misc_functions.R script.
A quick way to use all this is to clone the repo or download directly from github with the green ‘code’ button on the main repo page / ‘download zip’. Though all data used below loads directly from URLs, so don’t require it to be downloaded locally.
As the pre-bake page says, we’ve got the following to work with:
These are both rich datasets (though it’s worth exploring how the reginal GVA data is made to get a sense of its issues). Here, we’ll just run through a range of examples to show how to get started with digging into them.
See the left hand bar for other ways to use them, including a deeper dive into location quotients / proportion plots, and into GVA gap analysis.
Please let me know if you have any thoughts, ideas or code on other analyses to add etc, via the github issues or email danolner at gmail dot com).
Here’s some libraries, and the functions inside this repo we’ll use.
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)#for geo stuff
library(tmap)#for mapping 
library(zoo)#for making smoothed moving averages
library(patchwork)#combine ggplots easily
library(plotly)#For interactive plots

source('functions/misc_functions.R')

#Set ggplot theme
theme_set(theme_light())

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
text:
Looking at location quotients
Now let’s use location quotients (LQs) to see where goods and services are most concentrated across the UK.
This post goes into much more depth with LQs, looking at ways to compare places and break them down into 2D proportion plots. It has a full explanation of LQs - but briefly:

If the LQ > 1, that sector is relatively more concentrated in the region, compared to the UK
If the LQ < 1, it’s relatively less concentrated in the region, compared to the UK
… and the value says by how much e.g. an LQ of 2 would mean it’s twice as concentrated.

LQs also have a handy feature:

As the ONS Excel sheet on LQs make really clear, because (A/B)/(C/D) is equivalent to (A/C)/(B/D), the LQ actually captures two related ways of seeing the same thing: how relatively concentrated sectors are across a whole geography like the UK, and how concentrated within a subgeography like South Yorkshire they are. (See the table in the ONS document - numbers which can be read either across geographies or across sectors.)

(Note also: LQs only make sense for current prices data. Chained volume data can’t be summed, as each row is inflation-adjusted invididually and e.g. ITL3 zones or sectors don’t sum to larger geographies or SIC groupings because of that. LQs need to sum sectors and places to correctly work out proportions.)
First, using a function loaded above, this adds LQ details to the loaded CSV:

lq.latestyear <- add_location_quotient_and_proportions(
  itl3.ps %>% filter(year == max(year)),#use the latest year in the data
  regionvar = Region_name,
  lq_var = SIC07_description,
  valuevar = value
)

Then - ordering ITL3 zones by which has the highest goods-sector concentrations, comparing different places. Here, just outputting the ordered data and picking the top 15.

lq.latestyear %>% filter(
  SIC07_description == 'Goods sector'
  ) %>% 
  mutate(regional_percent = sector_regional_proportion *100) %>% 
  select(Region_name,regional_percent, LQ) %>% 
  arrange(-LQ) %>% 
  slice(1:15)

# A tibble: 15 × 3
   Region_name                          regional_percent    LQ
   <chr>                                           <dbl> <dbl>
 1 North and North East Lincolnshire                53.7  2.83
 2 Mid Ulster                                       50.5  2.66
 3 Flintshire and Wrexham                           48.7  2.57
 4 West Cumbria                                     44.0  2.32
 5 South and West Derbyshire                        40.7  2.15
 6 Durham CC                                        39.2  2.07
 7 Derby                                            37.1  1.95
 8 Mid and East Antrim                              35.9  1.89
 9 Northumberland                                   35.3  1.86
10 Fermanagh and Omagh                              35.2  1.85
11 Central Valleys                                  35.0  1.84
12 Mid Lancashire                                   34.9  1.84
13 Gwent Valleys                                    34.3  1.81
14 Armagh City, Banbridge and Craigavon             33.9  1.79
15 Kingston upon Hull, City of                      33.8  1.78


Services is of course the mirror image of this, and we could list them - but taking a look at a map of goods sector LQ is also a good way of seeing what’s going on. A couple of notes:

Log LQ is used as this keeps it symmetrical each side of zero, which makes the map a lot more legible (with the downside that log values aren’t as interpretable).
Zones with LQ < 1 for goods are highlighted in thicker black lines - making clear that more service-heavy places tend to be towns and cities (and a swathe of London and the South East).
Plotting an interactive map here so it’s easier to poke around / zoom in - change tmap_mode to ‘plot’ to just output as an image.

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
text:
Making a map

#Load ITL3 map geodata
itl3.geo <- st_read('data/ITL_geographies/International_Territorial_Level_3_January_2021_UK_BUC_V3_2022_6920195468392554877', quiet = T) 

#Check geo and data row matches... tick
#Names don't quite match between the two, random commas etc
# table(itl3.geo$ITL321CD %in% itl3.ps$ITL_code)

#Join map data to a subset of the GVA data
LQ_map <- itl3.geo %>% 
  right_join(
    lq.latestyear %>% filter(
      SIC07_description == 'Goods sector'
      ),
    by = c('ITL321CD'='ITL_code')
  )

tmap_mode('view')#Use 'plot' to just plot an image

#Make map for interactive viewing
tm_shape(LQ_map) +
  tm_polygons('LQ_log', n = 9, id = 'Region_name', fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "RdBu")) +
tm_shape(LQ_map %>% filter(LQ < 1)) + #Highlight LQ < 1 places by overlaying thicker lines
  tm_polygons(lwd = 2, alpha = 0, border.col = 'black', , id = 'Region_name') +
  tm_layout(title = 'LQ spread of\nGoods sector\nAcross ITL3 regions', legend.outside = T)

section: Using linear slopes to examine biggest growers and shrinkers
text:
Using linear slopes to examine biggest growers and shrinkers

#Use
#LQ_slopes %>% filter(slope==0)
#To see which didn't get slopes (all got slopes here but sometimes there'll be missing values)
LQ_slopes <- compute_slope_or_zero(
  data = itl3.ps, 
  Region_name, SIC07_description,#slopes will be found within whatever grouping vars are added here
  y = log(sector_regional_proportion), x = year
  # y = LQ_log, x = year
  ) %>% left_join(
    itl3.ps %>% select(Region_name,ITL_code) %>% distinct(), by = 'Region_name'#Add ITL code back in, so we can link to geodata below
  ) %>% 
  arrange(-slope) %>% 
  mutate(approx_percentchange_peryear = slope * 100)

Using that, we can ask: where does it look like the proportion of services sectors has grown the most? Just sorting by slope size:

LQ_slopes %>% filter(
  SIC07_description == 'Services sector'
  ) %>% 
  select(Region_name,approx_percentchange_peryear) %>% 
  arrange(-approx_percentchange_peryear) %>% 
  slice(1:15)

# A tibble: 15 × 2
   Region_name                     approx_percentchange_peryear
   <chr>                                                  <dbl>
 1 Mid and East Antrim                                    2.08 
 2 Essex Thames Gateway                                   1.24 
 3 Sandwell                                               1.05 
 4 East Lancashire                                        1.02 
 5 Clackmannanshire and Fife                              0.891
 6 Wolverhampton                                          0.889
 7 Stoke-on-Trent                                         0.852
 8 Solihull                                               0.848
 9 Scottish Borders                                       0.831
10 Darlington                                             0.818
11 West Lothian                                           0.776
12 Falkirk                                                0.718
13 Thurrock                                               0.714
14 Swindon                                                0.714
15 Hartlepool and Stockton-on-Tees                        0.694


We can make a map again, looking at what percentage change per year, on average, the slopes look like across the UK. There’s no obvious pattern to places where services have shrunk as a proportion of their economies - but as with the list above, East Antrim is an outlier. We’ll see in a second how much work “as a proportion” is doing…
(Note, not an interactive map as it appears tmap/leaflet can only display one per page at the moment - it’s changed back to ‘plot’ mode).

slopes_map <- itl3.geo %>% 
  right_join(
    LQ_slopes %>% filter(
      SIC07_description == 'Services sector'
      ),
    by = c('ITL321CD'='ITL_code')
  )


tmap_mode('plot')

#Make map
tm_shape(slopes_map) +
  tm_polygons('approx_percentchange_peryear', id = 'Region_name', fill.scale = tm_scale(values = "RdBu")) +
  tm_layout(title = 'Services sector approx. % GVA change per year, ITL3 regions', legend.outside = T)

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
section: Plotting time series for places where services grew/shrunk the most
text:
Plotting time series for places where services grew/shrunk the most
Let’s take a look at the actual datapoints for ‘percent of regional economy that’s services’, using the slopes data to extract the top (highest proportional growth) and bottom (highest prop shrinkage) slopes.

First, get the place names for top and bottom
Then in one ggplot for each of those, just look at the 1998 to latest datapoints
Using the excellent patchwork library to easily combine and title these two plots.


#Has already been ordered by slope, so can just filter and pull out
#We just want the place names, to then plot their slopes
topITL3names <- LQ_slopes %>%
  filter(SIC07_description == "Services sector") %>%
  slice_head(n = 12) %>% 
  select(Region_name) %>% 
  pull
  
bottomITL3names <- LQ_slopes %>%
  filter(SIC07_description == "Services sector") %>%
  slice_tail(n = 12) %>% 
  select(Region_name) %>% 
  pull
  


top.plot <- ggplot(itl3.ps %>%  
         mutate(regional_percent = sector_regional_proportion *100) %>% 
         filter(
           Region_name %in% topITL3names,
           SIC07_description == "Services sector"
           ), 
       aes(x = year, y = regional_percent, colour = fct_reorder(Region_name,-sector_regional_proportion) )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Paired', direction = 1) +
  ylab('Regional GVA percent') +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold')) +
  labs(colour = 'ITL region')


bottom.plot <- ggplot(itl3.ps %>%  
         mutate(regional_percent = sector_regional_proportion *100) %>% 
         filter(
           Region_name %in% bottomITL3names,
           SIC07_description == "Services sector"
           ),
       aes(x = year, y = regional_percent, colour = fct_reorder(Region_name,-sector_regional_proportion) )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Paired', direction = 1) +
  ylab('Regional GVA percent') +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold')) +
  labs(colour = 'ITL region')


top.plot / bottom.plot + plot_annotation(
  title = 'Change in proportion of service sectors, 1998-2022, top/bottom ITL3 zones'
)








Blimey - a couple of places really jump out from each plot, both inflecting around 2016. Mid and East Antrim in the ‘top proportion growers’ jumps hugely. Southampton equally has a massive drop - never far from a mid-80% service economy, it drops to below 70% before bouncing back a little. North / northeast Lincolnshire also sees a large drop - and appeared previously at the top of the “% goods sectors” list, with nearly 3 times higher proportion than the UK as a whole.
Let’s look at a couple of these, using different approaches and datasets.

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
section: Mid and East Antrim’s change over time
text:
Mid and East Antrim’s change over time
Mid/East Antrim’s apparently huge services jump highlights why proportional changes need to be treated carefully. What’s happening underneath that? Did services grow - or did goods and production drop, making services a bigger percent of Mid/East Antrim’s economy?
Let’s look at the chained volume data to find out; this will let us see actual sector volume changes over time, adjusted for inflation. We’ll separate production from services.
Note: “Mid and East Antrim” has been assigned to ‘place’ - “North and North East Lincolnshire” is commented out - change if you want to use the same code to explore that (or any other place). It’s quite the opposite story to Mid/East Antrim, if this data is right.

itl3.cv <- read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanOlner/RegionalEconomicTools/refs/heads/gh-pages/data/regionalGVA/regionalGVA_chainedvolume_ITL3_SIC_SECTION_LONG_2022.csv')

lookup.itl3 <- read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanOlner/RegionalEconomicTools/refs/heads/gh-pages/data/siclookup_forregionalGVAcategories_ITL3.csv')

itl3.cv <- itl3.cv %>% 
  left_join(
    lookup.itl3 %>% select(SIC07_code_sections,SIC07_code_three,SIC07_description_three) %>%
      rename(SIC07_code = SIC07_code_sections) %>% distinct(), 
    by = c('SIC07_code')
  )


place = "Mid and East Antrim"
#place = "North and North East Lincolnshire"

productionplot <- ggplot(itl3.cv %>%  
         filter(Region_name == place, SIC07_description_three=="Production sector"), 
       aes(x = year, y = value, colour = fct_reorder(SIC07_description,-value) )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Paired', direction = 1) +
  ylab('SIC section GVA (chained volume) ') +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold')) +
  labs(colour = 'SIC section') +
  facet_wrap(~SIC07_description_three)


servicesplot <- ggplot(itl3.cv %>%  
         filter(
           Region_name == place,
           SIC07_description_three=="Services sector",
           !qg('households|other service', SIC07_description)
           ), 
       aes(x = year, y = value, colour = fct_reorder(SIC07_description,-value) )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Paired', direction = 1) +
  ylab('SIC section GVA (chained volume) ') +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold')) +
  labs(colour = 'SIC section') +
  facet_wrap(~SIC07_description_three)

#Patchwork them together
productionplot / servicesplot + plot_annotation(
  title = paste0('Production vs services GVA (chained volume) in ', place)
)








So - while some service sectors have grown, it’s very clearly that huge drop in manufacturing that accounts for the relative percent growth in services. Manufacturing was by a very long way the broad sector with the highest output, but - if this data is right - it’s dropped off a cliff.
We can dig further by loading and looking at Mid/East Antrim’s 2 digit SIC codes for manufacturing, showing that the drop has mostly happened within a single 2 digit manufacturing category. And the drop appears to have been happening more or less every year of the data.
(Uncomment the log10 line to see another point: other much-smaller-GVA manufacturing SIC groupings have been affected in a similar way, with a post-2016 drop off.)

#Load 
itl3.cv <- read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanOlner/RegionalEconomicTools/refs/heads/gh-pages/data/regionalGVA/regionalGVA_chainedvolume_ITL3_SIC_2DIGIT_LONG_2022.csv')

itl3.cv  <- itl3.cv %>% 
  left_join(
    lookup.itl3 %>% select(SIC07_code,SIC07_code_sections,SIC07_description_sections) %>% distinct(), 
    by = c('SIC07_code')
  )


ggplot(itl3.cv %>%  
         filter(Region_name == place, SIC07_description_sections=="Manufacturing"), 
       aes(x = year, y = value, colour = fct_reorder(SIC07_description,-value) )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = 'Paired', direction = 1) +
  ylab('SIC GVA (chained volume) ') +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = 'bold')) +
  # scale_y_log10() +
  labs(colour = 'SIC 2 digit')

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
section: Southampton’s GVA versus job change over time: wigglyplot
text:
Southampton’s GVA versus job change over time: wigglyplot
Mid and East Antrim doesn’t have BRES jobs data - BRES doesn’t cover Northern Ireland. For ITL3 zones in Great Britain, though, we can use the joined GVA and BRES job data to see how each moved together.
BRES data begins in 2015, so the joined data loses the GVA data’s deeper history going back to 1998.
The following plot does this for Southampton’s SIC sections - directly plotting both chained volume GVA and full time job counts as they changed from 1998.
The first thing we do after loading the chained volume data: use the zoo library to make a moving average over time to more easily see the trends. (Note: in the function for the plot, the non-smoothed values are commented out if you want to see how messy that makes the plot!)
Doing this for 2015 to 2022 gives six smoothed datapoints.

gva.jobs.ITL3 <- read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DanOlner/RegionalEconomicTools/refs/heads/gh-pages/data/regionalGVA_plus_BRESjobcounts/regionalGVA_plus_BRESjobcounts_chainedvolume_ITL3_SIC_SECTION_MINUSimputedrent_2022.csv')

#Make a 3 year moving average
smoothband = 3

#Find GVA per FT job and add moving avs 
gva.jobs.ITL3 <- gva.jobs.ITL3 %>% 
  mutate(gvaperjob = gva/JOBCOUNT_FULLTIME) %>%
  # mutate(gvaperjobFT = gva/JOBCOUNT_ALLINEMPLOYMENT) %>% 
group_by(GEOGRAPHY_NAME,SIC07_description) %>%
  mutate(
  jobcount_movingav = rollapply(JOBCOUNT_FULLTIME,smoothband,mean,align='center',fill=NA),
  # jobcount_movingav = rollapply(JOBCOUNT_ALLINEMPLOYMENT,smoothband,mean,align='center',fill=NA),
  gva_movingav = rollapply(gva,smoothband,mean,align='center',fill=NA),
  `gva/job moving av` = rollapply(gvaperjob * 1000,smoothband,mean,align='center',fill=NA)
) %>% 
  ungroup()

Next, this function puts that into a 2D ‘wiggle’2 plot that shows every datapoint over time (2016 and 2021 are the start and end points, as the 3 year averages cover 2015-17 and 2020-2022).
It takes a bit of staring but it’s worth it to get a single-view idea of all major regional economic movements and what they mean.
(Note the option to change over and look at other places - North East Lincolnshire is very interesting on this plot.)

p <- twod_generictimeplot_multipletimepoints(
  df = gva.jobs.ITL3 %>% filter(
    qg('southampton',GEOGRAPHY_NAME),
    !qg('agri|constr',SIC07_description),
    jobcount_movingav > 2500
    ),
  category_var = SIC07_description,
  # x_var = gva,
  # y_var = JOBCOUNT_FULLTIME,
  # label_var = gvaperjobFT,
  x_var = gva_movingav,
  y_var = jobcount_movingav,
  label_var = `gva/job moving av`,
  timevar = DATE,
  times = c(2016:2021) 
)

p + theme(aspect.ratio=1) +
  # scale_x_log10() +
  # scale_y_log10() +
  xlab(paste0("GVA (",smoothband," year moving average)")) +
  ylab(paste0("Job count FT (",smoothband," year moving average)"))








What can we see here?

The likely explanation for Southampton’s proportional drop in service sectors: look at manufacturing (bottom of plot). It starts in 2016 (red dot, 2015-17 average) and ends in 2021 (2020-22 average, black dot), with each datapoint marked by a tiny arrow pointing along its change path.
Manufacturing GVA has pretty much exactly tripled over the time series (remember, this is chained volume, so adjusted for inflation - this is a real tripling of value, if the data’s right).
But jobs have increased much less (around 400 extra, starting at about 3400 in 2015-17). As a result, GVA per job has gone from 200K to 542K (see labels). Manufacturing has a much smaller job count than other SIC sections here, but it’s far ahead in GVA/job.
Going exactly the opposite way, Transportation/storage has a good chunk more jobs but - while it’s again slightly increased those numbers - GVA has been consistently dropping.
Compass quadrants (NE, NW etc) show which sectors had joint GVA and jobs growth (green / NE). Manufacturing is - just - in that category.

title: Intro to using ONS GVA and jobs data in R
section: So what’s going on with those places?
text:
So what’s going on with those places?
It appears to be a combination of genuine economic changes and ONS method alteration after publication of the Blue Book 2022. Southampton Data Observatory say:

“The ONS identified a change in the UK National Accounts that resulted in a long-term revision to the manufacturing of food, beverages and tobacco industry. This change happened to be concentrated in the Southampton area.”

GVA for overseas operations of firms based in Southampton previously hadn’t been included; now it is (see also here for Blue Book 2023).
While these changes don’t cause huge national shifts in GVA (although some) the regional impact varies - hence what we see in Southampton and Mid/East Antrim.
The ONS explain another key source of change here - a move towards using direct VAT data in addition to survey data, which has in some cases quite radically altered measured output:

“These upward revisions to manufacturing are driven by the incorporation of Value Added Tax (VAT) data for Quarter 3 2022 and updated data in other quarters. This is the case in particular in the manufacture of computer, electronic and optical products and manufacture of food products, beverages and tobacco.”

title: Regional GVA and job count data: easy squeezy versions
text:
What’s this?

Easy-access ONS regional gross value added (GVA) by SIC sector data, supplied as tidy CSVs: ITL2 & 3 geographies, and SIC industrial codes at 2-digit, Section (20 categories) and Production/Construction/Services, 1998 to most recent available year, 2022. (Original ONS excel, code, example use in R: location quotients / proportion plots.)
Same for BRES (the Business Register and Employment Survey) region-by-sector job count data, with extra-bonus higher accuracy values (see below). 2015 to latest year, 2023. (NOMIS page, code for API & wrangling.)
Those two linked together into single GVA/jobcount datasets (2015 to 2022), matching the GVA data’s bespoke 2-digit and section SIC categories for ITL3 (see below for more on that). (Code.)



See below the data for ‘Why’s this?’

There are also SIC lookup CSVs (three-group, sections, 2-digit) specific to the ONS regional GVA’s bespoke categorisations here for ITL2 and here for ITL3 (as well as an SIC lookup for the standard list here).

These CSVs are closest to the original ONS excel sheet. Code going from the xls to these is here.
GVA values are all in millions of pounds, same as the original.
As well as ITL2 and ITL3 geographical zones, there’s:

“3GROUPS”: SIC sectoral groupings for production, construction and services separately.
“SIC_SECTION”: 20 SIC top-level sections (SIC codes with letters A to T) (see SIC hierarchy). NOTE: the ITL2 data has all single letter sections A to T; ITL3 data has A/B and D/E combined into their own categories, so there are two fewer.
“SIC_2DIGIT”: 2 digit codes, the most granular level available in the regional GVA data. NOTE AGAIN: here, ONS combine a few of them, so these are are a smaller bespoke list in the GVA data. For ITL2 zones, there are 72 SIC categories. For ITL3 zones, there are 48 SIC categories.

There a couple of other choices of CSV type:

CP is “current prices”, CV is “chained volume”.
“Current prices” gives pound values at the time the data was collected, without inflation accounted for. Useful for analysing relative change and comparing places. And because it’s the actual price values at the time, your own groupings of places and sectors can be summed without problems.
“Chained Volume” adjusts for inflation - “by calculating the production volume for each year in the prices of a reference year. The resultant time-series of production figures has the effects of price changes removed.” Prices are set relative to 2019. So, absolute change over time can be analysed - e.g. “has sector x in place y grown at a more rapid rate than others?” (With current price data, we can only ask, “has sector x / place y grown relative to others? An entire sector may have shrunk, but one sector/place may still have relatively increased its proportion.)
Chained volume data cannot be summed by the user, you can’t add places or sectors together, as each has been chained together to produce values relative to the reference year. This means that for some of the data below, it’s not possible to supply a chained volume (CV) version because it relies on being able to add up values. CV is included where possible.

Lastly:

Long data has a single “year” column containing all years.
Wide data is in the same format as the original Excel sheet, with a column for each year.

This list doesn’t include 2 digit SICs as you can just remove the “imputed rent” row yourself from the first lot of data if you don’t want it. These datasets combine regional GVA and BRES job count data into single CSVs. They contain the same fields as the separate datasets above, but note these two points:

The newer post-Brexit ITL geographies for 2021 are the same as the previous EU-wide NUTS 2016 ones - apart from one small difference: ITL3 has “Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole”, NUTS 3 has “Bournemouth and Poole”. Christchurch moved from “Dorset” in the data in 2021. Due to the “chained volume GVA can’t be summed” issue, the solution used here is this: The ITL3 zones for “Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole” / “Dorset” / “Somerset” are replaced with the ITL2 zone that overlaps them all (“Dorset and Somerset”). title: Regional GVA and job count data: easy squeezy versions
text:
Why?

Main reason: contribute to reducing the effort / wrangling / wheel-reinventing needed to analyse UK regional economic data, including making sure all national data is together in one place, because any place needs comparing to others to understand it properly).
The ONS publish regional GVA data for the UK, covering a range of SIC sectors (2022 is the latest available year - the data’s here). It’s amazing data, presented in one handy place - but it needs some wrangling to get into an analyseable form, especially for use in R or similar.
This page provides easy-to-access copies from that dataset, with each useful dataset in its own CSV. It’ll be updated when the latest GVA data comes out.
Examples of analysing this data in R are in the left-hand bar. For instance, UK Sectors: LQs and proportion plots walks through using the data here to produce location quotients, maps and other plots.


Also:

UK regional/sectoral job count data is available via BRES (the Business Register and Employment Survey) on NOMIS. NOMIS is a brilliant platform, but again there are repeated steps usually needed before it’s in good shape for use. (And here we can also use NOMISR to get directly.)
It’s also possible to extract more accurate job count numbers by aggregating up from the most granular sector counts The BRES data below uses these more accurate counts.
So this page also has quick-access versions of all the most useful versions of the latest BRES data, including previously available years.



Also also:

It’s useful to have both regional GVA and job count values combined (for e.g. GVA per job analysis, or to have gva and job analysis using the same SIC categories and places) - so this page also has linked GVA and job count data.
There are several wrinkles with this data to get them to play nicely together that anyone using should be aware of - see details below.
Any thoughts on things that could be improved or that I’ve stuffed up, please let me know - either in the github issues or via email at danolner at gmail dot com (or any other contact methods listed top right on my code blog).



Automate!
Making data processing like this as automated and repeatable as possible makes it as open and useable as possible, which is a step towards quicker, more shareable analyses. As soon as new GVA or BRES data comes out, code from the repo can (hopefully!) be re-run painlessly5.
Quarto doc for this page is here.

title: Regional GVA and job count data: easy squeezy versions
text:
Footnotes


The split between full and part-time is more/less than 30 hours a week. The “in employment” category “includes employees plus the number of working owners. BRES therefore includes self-employed workers as long as they are registered for VAT or Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) schemes. Self employed people not registered for these, along with HM Forces and Government Supported trainees are excluded.”↩︎
Apart from one tiny difference - see the section describing the GVA/BRES joined datasets for more info - ITL and the most recent NUTS zones are the same, but the NUTS zones don’t have data past 2022, and the ITL zones have none prior to 2022 (they overlap one year).↩︎
Or I think so anyway. How come? The BRES rounding rules are applied to every SIC hierarchy the same - so 5 digit SICs are rounded the same as sections. Summing from 5-digit upwards - smaller average values here means smaller roundings applied - thus gives more granular job values. I’ve tested by checking the spread of the newer job counts around the original values, so e.g. comparing 2 digit SIC sums from this version and the values for 2 digit jobs in BRES itself. The new values spread evenly either side of the old, suggesting no introduced bias. Code for that test is in this script, in this section: ‘CHECK HOW THE “SECTION AND 2 DIGIT JOBCOUNTS SUMMED FROM 5 DIGIT” compare to the BRES original versions of 2 DIG and Sections’.↩︎
The ‘current price’ data could be summed, but the best that could be achieved there to keep a consistent time series would be a zone combining Dorset with Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole. For chained volume values, it has to be the larger ITL2 zone, for the reasons given. Rather than do both, here I’ve just used the one approach so all data is comparable directly.↩︎
Well, that’s the theory. The underlying data structures might stay the same, you never know…↩︎

title: Jobs/GVA elasticities for sectors in South Yorkshire
text:
These results estimate the elasticity between jobs and GVA for South Yorkshire e.g. “For every job added to the economy, GVA could change by…” (with 95% confidence intervals). (Log of difference in jobs is regressed on log of GVA differnce across pairs of years.)
Data comes from the difference between pairs of years for GVA and jobs. There isn’t enough data to get ITL2 vs SIC sections, but there’s enough for each separately (and ITL2 broken down by goods v services). Here, just pre-pandemic data is used too - most likely a more reliable take on the real jobs/GVA relationship (though COVID will have changed that).
To get South Yorkshire sector estimates, national sector elasticities are applied to South Yorkshire sectors (“If South Yorkshire sectors had national elasticities, then one extra SY job equals x GVA change”), and that is adjusted by the difference to the national mean for South Yorkshire as a whole, by goods v services, to reflect SY’s national position.
Public sectors have been removed from the analysis, because ONS deduces their GVA by multiplying jobs x regional wages. So trying to find GVA elasticities would be circular.
Finance is a highly modelled sector, GVA-wise, so treat with caution.
Mining is a tiny proportion of SY economy (~200 jobs) so elasticities likely to be volatile




Productive sectors (GVA per worker / per hour terms) may be inelastic to employment change - so adding new workers may not affect output as much as one might hope. This is most likely due to the ratio of workers to capital investment in those sector’s GVA. For example, this appears to be the case for ICT as a whole, as well as in South Yorkshire: it’s a highly productive sector but changes in employment lead to only weak GVA changes. Sheffield’s ICT sector is largely telecoms - a very capital intensive sector.
Some of these results are puzzling e.g. a low jobs/GVA elasticity for power sectors is to be expected given its huge capital intensity, but arts/entertainment is also low. Service sectors like that should have a more direct relationship between employment and output; why doesn’t it do so here? (See below on why post-COVID job/GVA losses appear to strengthen the elasticity in food/ents sectors).
Confidence intervals overlap a great deal. A lot of sectors’/places’ jobs <> GVA relationship are not very statistically separable from each other. This is a finding in itself - job investment may have quite even results regardless of focus.
Manufacturing does stand out in South Yorkshire however, with higher possible values for the job > GVA multiplier.

Question I don’t have a full answer for: what kinds of investment tend to be more capital/labour complementary (capital more likely to create jobs) that substituting (capital tends to destroy jobs)?




It doesn’t identify causation. Salaries are a large part of the GVA number, but GVA can also change due to non-worker/capital investment, or external economic factors. So a GVA increase can lead to job increases.
Capital investment can correlate to an increase or decrease in jobcount; the numbers here just try to pick up on the average direction of the relationship between jobcount and GVA change.

text:
This document contains the following sections - all accessible via the table of contents on the right hand side of this page. Click on a top-level heading to open up its subheadings.

A summary/synthesis of the findings
Connections to other sector strategies - including a detailed data driven link to the UK Industrial Strategy
Headlines from the data analysis including a sector-by-sector breakdown of sectors (examining strongest and other important sectors). Hover on figure references for a preview or click to jump to them.
A series of data sections used as the basis for the analysis - see the ‘data’ section at the top of the headlines below for a full explanation of what has been used.

Here are links to other sources used in the analysis below to look at Bradford’s sectors/clusters in context (all open in new tabs).

A couple of data catalogues with plots for the full range of sectors in Bradford. These are:

Full 5 digit SIC employment location quotients broken down by parent 2 digit SIC.
GVA vs job percent change 2D plots. These show how much (inflation-adjusted) GVA and job counts have changed between their 2015-2017 average and 2021-23 average for ITL3 zones, with Bradford highlighted. Putting GVA and job percent change on different axes also shows exactly how productivity (GVA per full-time job) has changed and whether productivity gains have included job gains or losses. A number of these are also included in the annexe and linked to throughout.

A set of treemaps showing the relative size of sectors in Bradford (as well as comparing Bradford to other ITL3s in West Yorkshire). These are:

Treemap for BRES job count data (2023) for West Yorkshire ITL3 zones including Bradford - sectors with matching colours. Click to drill down into place then 3 SIC levels (section, 2 digit and 5 digit).
Treemap for Companies House job count data (up to end of June 2025) for West Yorkshire ITL3 zones.

Companies House map showing most common broad sector per 100m^2 hex. This is useful for getting a sense of Bradford’s economic geography and the surrounding areas.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
Stand-out sectors
There are stand-out sectors in both the production and services categories, analysed in detail below in the data headlines section. The focus here is on sectors with strong growth trajectories and tradeability potential (which naturally aligns with Industrial Strategy goals). Those are:

Services:

Head offices/management consultancy
Finance
Legal/accounting
With ICT and real estate both arguably on this list
Engineering / tech testing an historically important sector - has such strong declining productivity, it is difficult to include in a ‘strongest’ list, but may well be an essential element of productivity success in connected sectors


With head offices/consultancy quite a lot lower productivity than either finance or legal/accounting, it gets to the top of this list because of its stand-out growth trajectory, in a sector recognised as important in the Industrial Strategy. Those three all align with the Industrial Strategy under the ‘Professional and Business Services’ (PBS) heading. Finance obviously includes large, long-established firms in Bradford - but there is also evident dynamism in SME firms that shows up in this year’s Companies House data. Legal/accounting has had ups and downs historically, but it is still some way ahead of national average productivity.
ICT is showing reasonable growth compared to other places in GB, but there is a disconnect between that and jobs growth (which may be shrinking, and is static in the Companies House data) and the sector is still relatively small. Again, however, it contains important Industrial Strategy firms that overlap with engineering in the IS-8 sector definitions.
Real estate appears to have very strong productivity even compared to the rest of GB, but identifying its source in the data is difficult - see its full subsection below. That makes it tricky to put in productivity or tradeablility context, but it needs noting.

Manufacturing/production:

Machinery & transport manufacture
The metals sector (including fabricated metal)
Textiles
(Building construction has notable productivity growth, and could be an important Industrial Strategy sector, but is low productivity compared to other WY local authorities).


Machinery & transport manufacture ticks several boxes that put it at the top of that list: steady productivity rise putting it higher than Leeds now, with increased output and job count, putting it on a par with the sector’s national average - not something many Northern places can say. Every subsector under this SIC are increasing their job concentration (with the majority in machine manufacture). Companies House shows a range of SMEs in this sector, though in the last year jobs growth hasn’t been large.
The metals sector is where many cutting edge firms like Produmax reside, and stands out strongly in the growth slope analysis, though its productivity faces issues. However, its job and GVA trajectory have steadily continued throughout the data time period.
Textiles is on this list partly due to raw job count, but also because it has historically been reasonably good productivity, and has West Yorkshire-wide support in its Local Growth Plan. In many ways its data is similar to the food manufacture sector (where strong jobs growth is evident in last year’s Companies House data) but the productivity gap between the two sectors is large, and Bradford’s food sector is tracking below other WY authorities (though the most recent data might suggest that’s changing). The raw numbers: textiles in Bradford is 62.4K per full time worker (85.5K GB average); food manufacture is 38.4K per full time (73.7K nationally).

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
Strategy context
The section below and the data section linking to Industrial Strategy sector definitions dig into the detail of how Bradford’s economy fits into other sector strategies. This is a short synthesis of points from those.
Where the UK Industrial Strategy focuses on strategic and high growth sectors, both the West Yorkshire LGP and LSIP are more focused on sectors that include large job numbers but may not necessarily have high productivity or tradeability. Two of the sectors identified in the LGP - food manufacture and chemicals - face intense productivity challenges, though the LGP does also argue eloquently for support of the textiles industry in the region.
Chemical production has had national issues, but as the section below details, Bradford jobs growth has been undermined by a severe productivity drop. There may be support for chemical production as a key part of the IndStrat’s focus on foundational production that underpins all other output, but Bradford’s chemicals productivity trajectory is on the lower end of anywhere in GB.
The LSIP also aims to support health and care sector skills development, and Bradford does have many private firms in those sectors that show up in the Companies House data, with a large number of jobs. However, it is difficult to check the productivity of these sectors; they are historically very low, but there is also a national data issue for parts of the sector that are public. At any rate, it is not likely to be a very tradeable sector (though it is of course hugely foundational and important).
The LSIP also identifies (and combines) engineering and advanced manufacturing - this is a canny combination given the historic challenges engineering has faced in Bradford, despite being an essential element for other aspects of manufacturing.
Both the LGP and LSIP pick out some high growth cluster firms (the LGP with a detailed Cluster Action Framework). The LGP provides a linked network diagram of high-growth cluster firms, but - in terms of the data here - it is quite broad, covering most sectors (some productive but not all e.g. logistics). It is is difficult in this data to pick out, for example, low carbon / clean tech firms; as the IndStrat dector definition page points out, there are no direct matching SIC codes, making it hard to track them.
That said, for SIC codes the IndStrat does supply, Bradford clearly has many strengths that align very well with the stand-out sectors identified here. It aligns, for instance, with PBS SMEs - offering “targeted and intensive” support, including to strengthen export work. As discussed below, there are some key ‘frontier’ manufacturing sectors where Bradford also has clear strengths, including its communications, space and other tech sectors.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
UK Industrial Strategy

Overview
The UK Industrial Strategy was released in 2025, with accompanying plans for 6 out of the 8 target “IS-8” sectors. It also has a sector definition list that provides SIC codes being targeted - top level sectors and ‘frontier’ subsectors (a few of which overlap; most do not). These range in specificity between 2 digit and 5 digit SIC codes.
As that webpage says, most of these SIC codes cannot capture the full range of possible firms the strategy aims to cover, and it also contains entire sections that SIC codes can’t cover at all - clean energy and certain digital sectors in particular. However, it does allow an analysis of which sectors are definitely within those industrial strategy categories. This section gathers job details for those specific sectors - a distinct range of types and breadth - and compares Bradford to the rest of the UK where possible, to see which sectors align with the industrial strategy and other analysis above. This is done for both BRES and Companies House job counts, to pick up on different job types.
This document has a data section (“UK INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY LINKAGE”) that pulls out Bradford sectors in this ‘IndStrat’ list - giving job counts, LQs and change over time from both BRES and Companies House data.
The table below lists the IS-8 broad sector headings. In the IndStrat plots, the abbreviations for these IS-8 headings appear before the sector name. Clean energy - as mentioned above - has no SIC codes and so can’t currently be matched. There are no matching defence sectors or firms in Bradford.

Points from the IndStrat LQ plots for Bradford
The IndStrat LQ plots pick out for Bradford which IS-8 sectors are more concentrated job-wise, what their trajectory is and what the job counts are. This section can be read in conjunction with the more detailed data/sector analysis below, from which it draws.
There are three sectors in particular identified below as being important to Bradford but facing productivity challenges that could benefit from support flowing from the industrial strategy: chemical production, head offices / management consultancy and architect/engineering/tech testing services. See the analysis below for a description of the history of these sectors.

Bradford has both manufacturing and service strengths that marry with the industrial strategy.
From those examined below, Bradford’s IS-8 overlaps are:

PBS: across a number of sectors, including legal services, accounting, head offices and management consultancy.
Finance: as well as banks, Companies House accounts picks out a very large number of holding companies in the finance category.
Advanced manufacturing: the machinery / equipment not elsewhere classified SIC covers a lot of advanced firms including space sectors, and is 3000 jobs in BRES. While architect/engineering/tech testing is technically PBS, it has important connections to production and faces challenges. Chemical production has already been mentioned as key to the industrial strategy but a nationally struggling sector.
Digital: electronic instuments/navigation isn’t a large number of jobs relatively, but it is likely a part of the larger advanced manufacturing / digital tech crossover.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
West Yorkshire Local Growth Plan
The LGP’s “priority one” is unlocking growth in sectors.
That page has a detailed outline of subsectors across West Yorkshire, and it argues for building on those with the largest job presence, including textiles and food manufacture, as well as chemicals. Each of these sectors are identified below as facing long-standing productivity challenges; here, other advanced manufacturing sectors are also highlighted as vital for Bradford (especially metals and machinery/transport manufacture - the WY LGP cites space tech too, a lot of which will be in these categories). Chemical production is a focus of the UK Industrial Strategy - including as part of its “foundational inputs” category - and so could potentially benefit the most, out of all high-job-count / low-output sectors listed here.
The LGP also singles out financial and professional services as vital, and for Bradford, the analysis below absolutely bears this out - though again, with some high growth slope sectors facing productivity issues (head offices), other Bradford strengths are in a much stronger position (legal/accounting) while Bradford finance is productive but possibly static (though Companies House data suggests a dynamic finance sector).
The high growth cluster analysis in the LGP puts “engineering … at the heart of these opportunities as a driver and foundation of growth.” As mentioned, engineering is an historic Bradford strength that is facing a long term productivity issue; understanding this better could help support this ‘cluster action’ approach.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
section: West Yorkshire LSIP (Local Skills Improvement Plan) published 2023
text:
West Yorkshire LSIP (Local Skills Improvement Plan) published 2023
Page 4 of the West Yorkshire LSIP says it aims “ro enable employers and individuals to access the technical skills they need to support growth, transformation and increased productivity in our key sectors, defined as:”

Health and Social Care
Engineering and Advanced Manufacturing
Financial and Professional Services
Low Carbon
Digital and Technology
Creative Industries
Education
Construction
Transport and Logistics

The analysis below digs further into engineering, advanced manufacturing and financial and professional services - all Bradford sector strengths, with differing productivity challenges, though these are especially notable in engineering.
Other sectors listed in LSIP could go into two categories:

Broad sectors where, with the data here, it is difficult to shed much light on productivity issues. Health and social care faces the same issues as other mainly-public sectors in the data - they have clearly grown to be the largest or one of the largest broad sectors, but public sector productivity analysis is difficult (partly because of how ONS calculate it at a regional level - they just use job count times regional job average to estimate GVA). This in no way negates the need to improve health and social care skills, it just makes it hard to analyse productivity data.

Companies House data does show that both health and social care have a very large private sector presence in Bradford (Figure 9, Figure 10 and plots from ?@fig-indivfirmsSY on to identify specific firms), so these could well benefit / be benefiting from from LSIP-related support.

Other sectors have not been picked out below for specific analysis, but are high job count with national-level productivity issues, and often not highly tradeable beyond Bradford. See for example the 2D GVA vs job plots for transport (Figure 37) and construction (Figure 36).

The following sections dig into what the data shows for Bradford’s sectors; plots and analyses follow that text.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
The data
Three main data sources are used here (and one other smaller ONS source for the hourly productivity plots).
The main three data sources are:

ONS regional GVA data at ITL3 geographies, up to 2023 (the most recent available data).
BRES (Business Register and Employment Survey) data for job counts by sector and place, again up to 2023 for the latest.
Data extracted from Companies House accounts for individual firms in the last year, between June 2024 and end of June 2025. This data only contains firms with a registered address in Bradford, so it misses all firms with ownership registered elsewhere (e.g. this includes Produmax, registered in Manchester). However, it can provide a highly granular and up-to-date picture of sector economies, including employment change in the last year.

For some analyses, regional GVA and BRES jobs data are linked. To do this, BRES jobs are binned into the smaller list of 44 SIC groupings that the ONS uses for the GVA data, so e.g. GVA per full time job can be examined. Where possible, the most granular sector breakdowns are used.
Lastly, the UK government’s Industrial Strategy sector definition list is used to examine how Bradford’s economy meshes with that strategy.
All code for this analysis is available here, and here for processing Companies House accounts.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
Service sectors

Strongest service sectors

The head offices and management consultancy sector (SIC 70, 2.3% of FT jobs, 2.7% of GVA; Figure 4) jumps out in several of the plots below (looking at 5 digit job counts for this sector, this is mostly ‘head office activities’ in Bradford). While not a very productivity sector overall, it has the strongest GVA and jobs growth slopes of any sector, averaging 15% GVA and 16.7% GVA per FT job growth from 2015 to 2023 (Figure 14), statistically separable from most other places, and becoming even stronger in more recent years (Figure 16). Plotting its GVA percent change (2015/17 to 2021/23 averages) against the same for jobs (Figure 22) shows (in the lighter diagonal corner) how its productivity gains have come from GVA growth mostly, but including a jobs increases, and that Bradford’s trajectory has been one of the strongest, percentage-wise. Figure 2 (last panel) shows output per worker for the sector has been historically low everywhere, but Bradford has seen a large jump in trend since COVID, and it is now some way above the average for other ITL3 zones in the data (50K per FT versus 36).

Location quotients for the sector show a contrast (Figure 4): GVA continuing to increase its concentration, but more recently Bradford’s jobs in this sector being less concentrated in Bradford than the GB average (though the jobs LQ has hovered between more and less over time). The last year’s Companies House (CH) data, though, sees the sector growing its job count more than any other in Bradford, and more than other West Yorkshire authorities for firms with 10+ employees (Figure 9) - only a small number of firms in CH (8 showing a 14.2% employee increase overall) but indicative of sector growth.

Finance should possibly be at the top of this list, as it is 5.4% of Bradford’s economy and 3.7% of its full time workforce (4900 jobs in BRES; Figure 4). However, it doesn’t stand out in comparison to other Bradford sectors or the rest of GB. For example, in its 2D GVA vs jobs percent change plot (Figure 30), while its productivity has risen, it’s only a little - though note, it is at least in the more positive half in that plot, compared to many other places with productivity drops (in the grey top left diagonal).

The ‘finance’ SIC category in the GVA data covers SICs 64 to 66 (finance, auxiliaries and insurance) - looking deeper into the BRES 2 and 5 digit lists, building societies are the largest job chunk (1200 / 0.85%) and have been concentrated in Bradford (near the top of UK concentration) for the full data time period. There are actually more jobs in the ‘banks’ category (2400, 1,8%) but that is only a little above the GB average. Financial auxiliary jobs have been shrinking in number, and statistically more than most other places (Figure 15) and insurance is a very small number of jobs.
Companies House data also shows strong jobs growth in the last year (only Wakefield ahead in WY) - 14 firms with 10+ employees going from 1434 to 1558 employees (an 8.65% increase, Figure 9). (CH data also shows over 300 “fewer than 10 employees”) firms / lone traders, Figure 10).

Legal and accounting is a stand-out related sector in the PBS (Professional and Business Services) category (average 3.2% of jobs in 2021-23, 1.8% of total). With historically very high output per FT worker in Bradford (Figure 2 panel 5), it has dropped more recently but is still very high - 93.5K per FT versus 78.4K average for other ITL3 zones, some way above the national average.

The sector has grown jobs only modestly over the data time period, but it started from a high GVA and jobs baseline. Digging into the 5 digit SICs for the sector, ‘accounting/auditing’ (1150 jobs in latest BRES year) has been growing its job concentration strongly - still below average GB concentration, but heading higher and very high output. BRES records 833 workers in ‘solicitors’, but the trajectory is not as strong as accounting.
Companies House data for the last year shows growth in “fewer than 10 employee” firms of 7.4% (now up to 670 employees), though 10+ employee firms have been fairly static.




Notes on other service sectors

Real estate has a high output per worker everywhere (with imputed rent removed, so this is purely real estate itself, not a reflection of rising house prices). This should arguably be in “strongest service sectors”, but it is difficult to discern from the data where the productivity is coming from. Exactly half of the job count in this sector is in ‘housing association renting’. Jobs are increasing in each of the other subsectors (real estate, agencies, other letting) which are another 1000 jobs and, looking in Companies House data, there are firms like Dacre, Son and Hartley who employ 100 people and are clearly strong. Job numbers have risen since 2015/17 but output hasn’t risen quite as quickly (see GVA vs jobs plot, Figure 31). The sector is also productive even by UK standards (195K per FT worker versus 167K). But in this data, it cannot be seen what role housing associations versus other real estate is playing in this.
The ICT sector in Bradford is relatively small as a proportion of GVA and jobs (though not tiny - it’s 1,800 jobs and 1.73% of the economy). But after a fairly stagnant productivity path (Figure 2 panel 3), the sector has seen a productivity jump in more recent years (showing up as both reasonable GVA and jobs growth over the whole data period; Figure 28), putting it closer to the national average (76.8K per FT worker versus 86.K, 2021-23 average). This stronger growth trend than around 45% of other places puts it second only to Leeds in a West Yorkshire productivity ranking, and continuing to climb. Reading the LQ plot for GVA and jobs (Figure 4) it appears its GVA concentration - steady for a long time - is more recently going up, but possibly with a decline in job concentration. In the last year in the Companies House data, jobs are static (Leeds has grown; other WY local authorities have shrunk). So a mixed picture in a possibly important sector that aligns with the Industrial Strategy.
It is tricky to define architecture/engineering/tech testing’s place in Bradford (SIC 71). It is a large chunk of Bradford’s economy - more than 2000 jobs, 1.5% of full time workforce in latest BRES year, and has historically kept around the same number. However - while its GVA per worker in Figure 2 was very high in 2015-17, it has dropped off constantly since (while other places in WY have slowly climbed), now approaching the same output per worker as head offices / consultancy (though it is still above the average of other ITL3s). Jobs in the sector have grown in most places, but Bradford is some way into the group where GVA has dropped (Figure 23). There has been a jump in job numbers in the most recent data but no GVA jump, suggesting productivity continues to decline. Companies House shows a large number of SMEs in the sector, with modest jobs growth. But this sector (despite technically being under a ‘services’ heading) is obviously important to manufacturing and other productive output.

What factors underpin this steady slope? This data isn’t able to say directly, but identifying what’s happening here could be a first step to addressing it.

Utilities and power (5.7% of Bradford’s GVA, 2500 jobs in BRES) are tricky sectors to analyse. While the sector appears highly productive in Bradford (187K per FT job versus 138K GB average), differences in this sector largely come down to the capital intensity of the sector. There can be innovative frontier firms in these SIC codes, but the fact that very few firms in these sectors appear in the Companies House data suggests this sector is largely external utilities in the area, and could be difficult to affect.
Research / advertising, while apparently a high productivity sector, is fewer than 300 jobs, and this SIC misses other places where important research activity takes place.
Other professional, scientific and technical activities (“Other PSTech”, so any other apart from head offices, consultancy, legal, engineering - see the BRES job treemap for ‘professional/sci/techn’) appears productive, but is only a very small number of jobs. Bradford has been following the same trajectory as West Yorkshire, output per worker growing, and this is bucking the national trend where in places with more than 1% GVA in this sector, jobs have grown but productivity dropped. But it’s a very small sector.
Office administration and business support activities (“Admin” in the plots below; distinct from “public admin”) is not highly productive but its trajectory is worth noting. As Figure 32 shows, its jobs/GVA combination has led to a low but steady GVA per FT job increase (where a lot of other places have seen declines). The fact that this sector is so many jobs (3200 average 2021-23), and its connections with other PBS sectors, makes it worth noting.

title: Bradford sectors and clusters: past, present
text:
Manufacturing / production sectors
Despite an overall decline in the proportion of Bradford’s broad manufacturing economy (in line with the most of the rest of the UK and West Yorkshire, Figure 1), there is important production sector activity to highlight.

Strongest sectors

The machinery and transport manufacture sector (SIC 28-30, ~2.5% of jobs in 2021-23 average) has been growing in productivity since 2015/17, on a quite different upward trajectory from the rest of West Yorkshire (Figure 2 panel 4). It has been growing as a proportion of GVA and jobs in Bradford and its GVA has been rising steadily in the ‘increasing productivity’ zone (Figure 25) where most other places have seen productivity drops. It is now at or near the UK average sector productivity - a rare position for a Northern manufacturing sector (though Companies House data for the last year doesn’t show quite as strong performance).

Two thirds of these jobs are in machinery manufacturing, and every 5 digit subsector in that is increasing in concentration (only a tiny proportion in motor vehicles, according to BRES).

Metals sectors (SIC 2 digit 13-15) has a high LQ and ~2.6% of Bradford jobs (Figure 3). It has had continuous GVA and jobs growth - an average of 4.1% yearly GVA growth (1.1-6.9%, Figure 14) from 2015, increasing more since 2019. This covers many cutting-edge firms like Produmax, who classify themselves as ‘manufacture of other fabricated metal products’. (The 5 digit SIC jobs breakdown for fabricated metals shows this category is where the largest chunk of the fab metals jobs are in Bradford; BRES doesn’t record many jobs in basic metals).

However, the metals sector has low average output per worker. As the 2D GVA/jobs plots for metals shows (Figure 24), the sector has maintained an output increase alongside its productivity - right in the centre of other places seeing productivity losses and gains. This mean its productivity (gva/job) hasn’t actually changed much, while job and GVA values have both increased by more than 60% since 2015/17.

Textiles continue to grow GVA and jobs concentration (GVA more than jobs, Figure 3) though the sector isn’t quite 1% of total full time jobs. Companies House data, however, suggests the sector is probably larger than BRES’ survey is picking up on - there are nearly 1000 jobs in apparel firms in CH (BRES finds only 20) - so it may well be more like 2% of total jobs.

Historically, it has been higher than average GVA per job for Bradford, with all West Yorkshire authorities very close in output - but this has declined since COVID (Figure 2) and is now almost exactly average for Bradford but a little below UK average for the sector. The 2D GVA/job plot for textiles (Figure 26) shines some light on this. In the very few UK places where textiles are more than 1% of the economy, none have better productivity in 2021/23 than they did in 2015/17. Some (e.g. Calderdale/Kirklees) have seen jobs increase while GVA has dropped. Along with Blackburn, Bradford is doing relatively well on this metric - growth continues though with apparent productivity issues.




Notes on other manufacturing/production sectors

As Bradford’s largest 2-digit sector by job count, Food/beverage manufacturing has 3.6% of full time employers according to BRES, and 2.5% of its GVA. Worker growth looks especially strong in the last year in the Companies House data: the 14 firms with 10+ employees have grown nearly 9% (Figure 9) and 74 microfirms with fewer than 10 employees have gone from 212 to 281 employees (Figure 10), both higher than the rest of West Yorkshire. However, the sector overall has seen declining productivity, and Bradford’s GVA per worker is at the lower end for West Yorkshire (along with Leeds - the other authorities are higher; Figure 2). As the GVA vs jobs 2D plot for the sector shows (Figure 34), most places have seen job increases with either GVA shrinkage or too slow GVA growth for productivity gains; Bradford’s GVA growth in the sector has been static.
Bradford’s chemicals industry (SIC 19-23) has a similar pattern to architecture/engineering/tech testing - except in chemicals, job numbers continue to grow while GVA drops. Jobs have yo-yo’d but have been mostly rising in recent years - but GVA has dropped, leading to worsening productivity. Demand issues in recent years accounts for some of this (see e.g. this report) - but this pattern of GVA decline has been in progress from 2015-17. 5 digit chemical sectors are mostly seeing jobs growth - rubber/plastic jobs increasing strongly (700+ now in two subsectors) and chemical manufacturing jobs in most subsectors continue to grow too. But - see Figure 33 - Bradford has seen one of the largest output drops in GB (while, as everywhere else, seeing job numbers rise). This is clearly a national issue, but Bradford seems especially vulnerable.
Construction of buildings (“Buildings” in the plots, SIC 41) is worth noting for its improving productivity (GVA growing faster than jobs but both growing, Figure 29). The West Yorkshire pattern in Figure 2 (panel 3) for output per full time job shows the region moving together, though Bradford is at the bottom of the sector’s GVA per worker here - but it is also following the recent rise seen across the region.

The rest of this document provides ways to see and interact with the data used in this analysis.

These plots use linked regional GVA and BRES jobs data to examine productivity, output and job changes. To make this link, sector categories have to be reduced to those in the ONS GVA data (46 categories rather than the full 88 two digit SICs).
These are measured in GVA per full time job (GVA / jobs), using inflation-adjusted (chained volume) GVA.
BRES does contain more detail - more on that below and in the separate BRES 5 digit breakdown.
GVA per job as a measure needs some caution: output is also due to other productive factors, so high capital intensity sectors (power, telecoms, other ICT though not all) can appear overly productive per worker. It’s more representative for service sectors where an employee’s output more clearly correlates to total output, such as legal services.

text:
Location quotients for GVA and jobs in 2 digit SIC sectors: most recent and change over time
These LQ plots show location quotients for linked GVA and jobs data for Bradford, overlaid on top of LQs for all other ITL3 zones, to give a sense of what the spread is across Great Britain.
A location quotient is the ratio of a place’s sector proportion to its national proportion. So e.g. if manufacturing in Bradford made up 20% of its economy compared to maufacturing being 10% of the UK economy, its LQ in Bradford would be 2.
Here’s an explanation of how to read these location quotient plots:

Location quotients for sectoral GVA in the selected region
Sectors to the right of the blue line are more concentrated in this region when compared to the national average. (e.g. LQ = 10, it is 10x more concentrated). To the left are less concentrated than nationally.
Green circles have been increasing in concentration over time (larger circles increasing the most)
Red circles have been decreasing in concentration over time (larger circles decreasing the most)
Black horizontal lines show the min and max of concentration in the data’s history (from 2015 to 2023) (so, often, large green circles will be at the right of this line because sector concentration has been steadily increasing)
Per sector GVA money amounts and percent of that region’s entire economy are shown on the right.

title: Sheffield: GVA vs jobs 2D percent change plots
text:
These plots show percent change in chained volume GVA and job count on different axes, with Sheffield’s change overlaid in blue and job count plus percent of regional economy included in title (for the most recent year). It uses a 3 year moving average to smooth out jumps.
Only places where a sector makes up 1.5% or more of the economy are included - except for Sheffield, which is included in all plots.
This is done for the shorter 2 digit SIC categories in the regional GVA data, joined to BRES jobs data.
Any arrows in the top left grey diagonal section will have seen productivity drops (measured as GVA per FT job) over that time. In the bottom left diagonal, productivity went up.
Arrows in the bottom right quadrant have seen a combination of productivity increases with job decreases.
NOTE: All sectors are included even if they’re very small proportions of Sheffield’s economy - so percent changes could appear large for very tiny sectors. Look at the job count in the title to check. Including them all for completeness.

title: South Yorkshire creative & cultural industries: data from BRES and Companies House (October 2025)
text:
This web report examines data for Sheffield, Barnsley, Doncaster and Rotherham for sectors that are part of the UK Industrial Strategy definition of the creative and cultural industries (CCI). (See below for more info on the Industrial Strategy.)
As well as a short overview of the jobs and GVA history of South Yorkshire for CCI, each place is examined using location quotient (LQ) plots, placing them in the context of the UK’s core cities.
For the LQ analysis, two data sources with different strengths and weaknesses are used, to triangulate a fuller picture:

Business Register and Employment Survey (BRES) from 2015 to 2024, job counts. (2024 data was released 28th October.) The survey captures larger firms and their related sites, as well as smaller firms, but sample sizes become small at granular levels, so it can miss the full picture and is volatile between years.
Companies House (CH) firm level data, scraped for accounts submitted between September 2024 and end of September 2025. CH data’s main weakness: it records only firms HQ’d in South Yorkshire. But it captures a sizeable proportion of economic activity, and can often indicate (comparing to BRES) which sectors are more ‘home grown’ (a high CH / BRES ratio) and sometimes pick up on jobs BRES misses, as it’s not sample based. Here, it can also only compare job counts from when accounts were submitted and a year previously.

These are the following sections (see also table of contents on the right):

Some headlines from the analysis follow next.
Existing UKRI CCI clusters are listed.
An overview of the UK Industrial Strategy.
Data on the history of CCI in South Yorkshire (compared to core cities).
Bullet points on the location quotient results for the four places.
Full location quotient plot results.

title: Economic collaboration across Bradford and Leeds: what does the latest sector data show?
text:
This report digs into the economic connection between Bradford and Leeds from 1998 to the present day, putting it in a national context. It uses the latest ONS and Companies House data. The next section explores that data in detail. There are links to each chunk of analysis on the right, or scroll through them below. (Also, hover over figure citations for previews.) Open data and code for this report can be found here.

Over the last twenty five years, the economies of Bradford and Leeds have converged more deeply. Finance is a prime example, where both cities have grown together. In this year’s Companies House data, finance job growth continues in a good mix of micro and larger firms, with “sophisticated supply chains” identified by Metro Dynamics (2017) still developing, and Bradford’s job growth ahead of UK core cities.
Cultural and creative industries have sustained through tough times and are now thriving, helping to act as a “catalyst for inclusive growth”1, building on initiatives like Bradford’s UNESCO City of Film status and Leeds’ 2023 Year of Culture. In Leeds, the sector is more productive in purely economic terms than the UK average. Companies House data shows strong growth continues in these sectors in the most recent year, especially in smaller firms, with Bradford near the top of employment growth, on a par with Manchester.
Information and communication technology (ICT) has been growing everywhere in the UK for the past two decades, but Leeds’ and Bradford’s ICT output has grown significantly more than 59% and 45% of other places, respectively, suggesting ICT is growing together across both and deeply connected.
Leeds’ business services continue to grow in strength and specialisation, but Bradford’s finance, legal and technical sector growth suggests both places are benefiting from agglomeration. Sectors connected to the region’s learning and innovation have also drawn closer together economically, in both education and scientific/technical output.
Both cities’ health sectors have grown in tandem (to become 10% and 15% of Leeds’ and Bradford’s economies), and that growth continues in the last year in the private sector, with Bradford’s companies house jobs count now not far behind Leeds.
Commuter flows between the two cities affirms Bradford’s “strong functional relationship with Leeds” with “high flows of young qualified Bradford residents working in Leeds, many in the large global and UK consulting, accounting, insurance and financial services sector companies with presence there” (Metro Dynamics 20172).
This picture challenges any simple core/periphery take. Productivity analysis does show Leeds has higher per worker output in several sectors, but both are very close across many of them, and have historically moved in lockstep – with Bradford’s productivity higher in some key sectors like scientific /technical, and ICT productivity some way ahead of the UK average.
This level of economic integration has developed despite transport connectivity, not because of it. It has shaped which parts of the two cities have been able to connect the most and thus benefit from linkages. Several recent analyses (see e.g. Stansbury et al 20233) have reinforced the case that UK transport constrains core cities and their linked job markets. Addressing this impacts the whole economy, including cultural and creative sectors: “Poor transport connectivity can act as a barrier to people participating in culture”4 both from within Leeds and Bradford’s communities, and from outside the area.
The Northern Powerhouse Rail assessment’s analysis suggested that better “connection between Leeds, Bradford and Manchester can alone potentially increase productivity by 6%, raise the employment rate by 1.5% and increase gross value added (GVA) in the north by about 8% over 10 years” (Mott McDonald p.45). This report points to the deep connections between Bradford and Leeds’ innovation and research systems, as well as their complementary service infrastructure, and the co-benefits that can underpin. A step change in transport connectivity could lead to a qualitatively different level of agglomeration built on that, taking both cities beyond the kind of numbers NPR cite. Recent jobs growth evident in the Companies House data indicates what direction the region could go in, especially if building on wider ‘corridors of opportunity’ across West Yorkshire’s economy (see Companies House analysis below of growth across the region’s five local authorities).
